newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin says Russia has learned from 1993 clashes.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin says Russia has learned from 1993 clashes.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, speaking on the third anniversary of a bloody hardline uprising in Moscow, said both the Kremlin and the opposition had learned their lessons and should work to boost stability.

"The country came to the very edge of the abyss of civil war in those tragic days," Yeltsin said in a written statement marking the events of October 3 and 4, 1993, when he used tanks to crush a rebellion by hardline members of parliament.
"This happened because of a most acute confrontation between Russia's organs of authority."
He held out hope that all those involved in the standoff had drawn the right conclusions and that this would ensure political stability.

"Both the authorities and the opposition have drawn lessons from those grave events," he said. "Let us do everything to strengthen it, to ensure that those tragic events never happen in our land again."

Nearly two years after the collapse of the Soviet Union, on September 21, 1993, Yeltsin ordered the dissolution of the Russian parliament which was blocking his attempts to introduce a new constitution.
The deputies refused and remained barricaded in the White House parliament building.
On October 3, thousands of supporters of the rebel deputies went on the rampage in the capital, capturing the city council building and attacking the main television centre.
The following day, Yeltsin's tanks opened fire on the parliament building and pounded the deputies into submission. About 140 people were killed in two days of clashes.

The following December, Yeltsin won a referendum on a new constitution giving him huge powers. But a parliamentary election in 1995 returned a largely hostile lower chamber of parliament with the communists the largest single party.
Since 1993 Russia has been bogged down in a war in Chechnya which has killed tens of thousands of people, but outside the Caucasus domestic politics have been largely free of violence.
